How to Spot a Fake Driver License in Under Five Minutes

Seven physical tests that separate a printed licence from a real one, and the three questions that expose a seller who has never held the document.

A fake licence fails on physics before it fails on data. That is the useful part, because physics is something you can test on a kitchen table in daylight while the seller waits.

Start with the ghost image. Every modern licence carries a faint secondary portrait, usually offset from the main photo and printed in a tone that disappears at a shallow angle. On a colour photocopy it flattens into a grey patch that stays visible at every angle. Tilt the card through forty degrees and watch for the change.

Next is microprint. The signature line, the border or a strip beneath the photo is set in text around one point high. On a real card it resolves into letters under a loupe. On a copy it collapses into a dotted line. A ten pound jeweller loupe settles this in seconds and no seller can talk around it.

Third is the substrate. Polycarbonate cards flex and spring back. Teslin and PVC feel different again but both are dense and slightly warm to the touch. Paper laminated between two sheets is thinner, flexes further and clicks when tapped. Ask the seller to tap the card on video call and listen.

Fourth is the UV layer. Every authority in the developed world prints UV ink, usually a flag, a crest or a repeating pattern across the data field. Under a cheap UV torch it appears sharp and saturated. A print shows nothing, or shows a dull bloom where the paper was coated.

Fifth is the number. Licence numbers are constructed, not random. They encode surname, birth date, issue sequence or a check digit depending on the country. Break the rule and the card is wrong regardless of how good the print is. Look up the format for the issuing state before you look at any photo.

Sixth is the category grid. This is the hardest part of a licence to typeset convincingly, because the rows are fixed, the font is specific and the alignment is tight. Fakes cram categories, use the wrong weight, or leave a row empty that should carry a restriction code.

Seventh is the address. Fakes usually inherit the address from the real card they were copied from, so the postcode will be correct for the wrong street or the state will contradict the header. Compare the postcode against the issuing office area, not against the street.

Quick answers

Now the three questions. Which office issued it, and what is the district code. What is the check digit rule for this state. And what does the card look like under UV. A seller holding real stock answers all three without notes. A reseller pauses on the second and improvises on the third.

What if the seller only has photos?

Then run the tests you can run on photos, which are the number, the category grid and the address consistency, and ask for a UV shot before paying.

Is a perfect fake possible?

Yes, with real stock and the right printer. That is why the number and the register matter more than the print quality once you are past the obvious tells.
